item.title: Anthony Davis (34 points), Wizards ride 21-2 surge to upend Bucks
item.description: Anthony Davis scored 34 points and grabbed 12 rebounds to lead the Washington Wizards to a 128-116 victory over the visiting Milwaukee Bucks in the teams' season opener Wednesday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Anthony Davis scored 34 points and grabbed 12 rebounds to lead the Washington Wizards to a 128-116 victory over the visiting Milwaukee Bucks in the teams' season opener Wednesday night. Trae Young added 20 points and a game-high 13 assists for the Wizards, while Kyshawn George scored 18 points. In their first game with Milwaukee after being included in the offseason trade that sent Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami, Tyler Herro led the Bucks with 24 points and Jaime Jaquez Jr. scored 22. Fellow former Heat player Kasparas Jakucionis added 15 points off the bench. Leading 93-90 entering the fourth quarter, Washington took over in front of its home crowd. After trailing by as many as eight, the Wizards went on a 21-2 run in the fourth to build a 111-98 lead. Washington opened the quarter by making its first nine shots from the floor. The scoring in the fourth came from a variety of sources, with seven players posting at least four points as Washington outscored Milwaukee 38-23 to secure the victory. The Wizards did most of their damage without the 3-pointer. They made just three shots from beyond the arc in the second half while scoring 77 points. Davis made his presence felt early, scoring 10 points and grabbing six rebounds in the first quarter. The Wizards took a 25-23 lead into the second. Milwaukee bounced back in the second, outscoring Washington 33-26 behind seven points from Herro, who also scored seven in the first quarter. The Bucks led 56-51 at halftime despite shooting 5-for-17 from 3-point range. Washington was 3-for-17. The shooting improved in the third, as Milwaukee went 6-for-11 from beyond the arc and was led by Jaquez's 10 points. However, another dominant stretch from Davis, who scored 18 points, helped Washington win the quarter 39-37 and take a 93-90 lead into the fourth. Washington has won four straight games against Milwaukee after taking the final three meetings last season, snapping the Bucks' seven-year winning streak in the season series. --Field Level Media

item.title: Dip in the dollar takes a breather with Fed in focus
item.description: A downdraft in the dollar took a pause on Thursday as investors began hunkering down ahead of a slew of central bank meetings next week, where hawkish holds are expected on interest rates in Japan, the US and Europe.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A downdraft in the dollar took a pause on Thursday as investors began hunkering down ahead of a slew of central bank meetings next week, where hawkish holds are expected on interest rates in Japan, the US and Europe. The currency market is long the dollar on the assumption the AI boom keeps the US economy humming and that strong growth supports interest rates staying higher for longer. Recent gains for sterling and currencies in Canada, Australia and New Zealand, all of which have lately touched their highest on the dollar in several weeks, suggest dollar bets have been pared a bit, though moves on Thursday were slight. Sterling , which hit a one-month high of $1.3409 earlier in the week, has been supported hotter-than-expected British inflation and held at $1.33955. The Australian dollar , which made a three-week top on Wednesday, is hanging on above 70 US cents at $0.7025, while expectations for a rate hike next week in New Zealand hoisting the kiwi to a one-month high of $0.5709. Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said on Wednesday that the inflation outlook was looking "materially worse" in part due to high oil prices, pushing up market bets on whether the next hike in Australia comes as soon as next month. The Bank of Canada is also expected to hike next week and the loonie was supported near a one-month top of C$1.4032 per dollar. The euro and yen have settled into tight ranges, with the threat of intervention and prospect of rate hikes holding Japan's currency around 158 to the dollar . The euro has spent about a month on the slide, emerging as a favoured channel for putting a bet on a stronger dollar, as fiscal concerns in France and Europe's energy fragility attract short sellers. French 10-year yields hit their highest since 2022 on Wednesday as weekend unrest across France, fuelled in part by cuts to public services, has highlighted how politically difficult it will be to bring budget deficits under control. But aside from a brief dip in the thin trade of Monday morning in Asia, the euro has kept fairly steady above $1.12. "The euro cannot sell off—and it cannot rally," said Spectra Markets' president Brent Donnelly. "We are in a stalemate where the overhang of bad news just about perfectly offsets the market positioning." The European Central Bank is expected to hold its benchmark rate at 2.5% next week, though a hike is all but priced in before the year's end. Markets have priced a hold in Tokyo, too, with the next hike — to 1.5% — expected early next year. The Federal Reserve is seen on hold in October, with the Fed funds rate window at 3.75-4%, but hiking in December.

item.title: Meta strikes deal to keep Zuckerberg in California after wealth tax concerns
item.description: Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him living in California after the CEO warned he was considering leaving the state that houses the company's headquarters if voters pass a wealth tax proposal next month.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Méndez
item.content:encoded: Meta Platforms (META.O) has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him living in California after the CEO warned he was considering leaving the state that houses the company's headquarters if voters pass a wealth tax proposal next month. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will get non-voting shares he can sell to potentially foot a multi-billion-dollar tax bill in the event the proposal is approved, in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, Meta said on Wednesday. Zuckerberg, the world's sixth richest person according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because Proposition 40, a ballot measure dubbed the "California wealth tax", could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. Proposition 40, which asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5% [USN:L6N4511DT TEXT:"tax"] on the state's billionaires, is far from certain to pass, political analysts say. The state is home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively worth upwards of $2 trillion. Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of about $240 billion, can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill without losing voting control. The company [USN:L4N4671S3 TEXT:"said"] on Wednesday it will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively resulting in a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg's control. Meta's long-term forecasts, as described in the filing, showed it would need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years, beginning as early as fall 2026, as it expects to need capital to finance its AI-related growth plan. The parent of Facebook and Instagram said a special committee of its board concluded it was "critically important" that Zuckerberg remain in a leadership role and continue to manage the company from its California headquarters, particularly during what it described as "unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry" driven by AI.

item.title: Canada's Carney visits Turkey in push to ease US trade dependence
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney will meet President Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey on Thursday, marking the first bilateral visit by a Canadian leader, as he seeks to deepen trade with other "middle powers" and ease dependence on the US.
item.dc:creator: Maria Cheng
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Mark Carney will meet President Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey on Thursday, marking the [USN:L6N45N1A5 TEXT:"first bilateral visit"] by a Canadian leader, as he seeks to deepen trade with other "middle powers" and ease dependence on the US. Carney and Erdogan are [USN:L8N4660GU TEXT:"expected to sign"] a declaration deepening cooperation in four areas including defense and energy, a person briefed on the matter said. Carney is on a global trade blitz that he hopes will help buffer Canada from a [USN:SPN44J009 TEXT:"trade war"] with the US, where President Donald Trump has applied sweeping tariffs and questioned the neighboring country's sovereignty. NATO member Turkey seeks new investment and collaboration for its burgeoning defence industry, new nuclear power plants and mining sector. Carney's office said the visit aims “to position Canada as a key partner in trade and investment". Although trade between Canada and Turkey is tiny – Turkey accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada’s total merchandise trade or C$4.34 billion ($3.09 billion) – bilateral trade has risen by nearly 50% in the past five years. “This trip is part of the geopolitical necessity of signaling to Americans that we are not sitting around waiting for them,” said Bessma Momani, professor of political science at the University of Waterloo. In the last year, Canada has signed more than 20 trade deals as part of Carney’s push to double non-US exports in the next decade. He flew to Beijing in January to reset fractured relations with [USN:P8N3X30AH TEXT:"China"], striking a deal that slashed tariffs on electric vehicles and canola. Despite criticism that China is a security risk, given Canadian authorities previously found China had interfered in at least two federal elections, Carney has described China as a “more predictable” trading partner than the US. However, Canada still sends nearly 70% of exports to the US. Turkey's crackdown on the opposition since 2024, and arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community have drawn criticism. But Carney has focused less on rights than predecessors. “Carney will have to walk a very fine line in Turkey between opening new economic possibilities for Canada while trying to maintain Canada’s middle power role in fighting for equality,” said Anna Agathangelou, a professor of politics at York University. Ankara says the judiciary is independent, denying that investigations or court cases are politically motivated. At the NATO leaders' summit in July, Carney and Erdogan [USN:FWN43909C TEXT:"launched negotiations"] for a free-trade agreement, where Turkey also agreed to join Canada’s Defence, Security and Resilience Bank as a founding member. Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis ATRL.TO as well as South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants. In 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations. Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkey, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry. ($1 = 1.4052 Canadian dollars)

item.title: Japan's strong-armed $21 bln chip bet is low risk
item.description: Tokyo is funding two US factories and will share the profits with Washington under a trade pact. Returns on making low-end commoditised chips will underwhelm. Still, Abu Dhabi's GlobalFoundries is a safe partner and the deal could shore up supply chains at Japanese automakers.
item.dc:creator: Robyn Mak
item.content:encoded: Being bullied into a $21 billion deal is hardly ideal but that's the situation Tokyo finds itself in after agreeing to fund up to two new chip factories in the US. It falls under a $550 billion investment pact it struck last year with Washington in return for lower US tariffs on Japanese imports and as a way of [USN:L4N46102G TEXT:"dealing with"] President Donald Trump. At least for this venture, the risks look as low as the returns. The biggest winner is $26 billion GlobalFoundries (GFS.O) , owned by Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala. The contract chipmaker will construct and operate the first $10 billion factory without having to commit a single dollar of capital. In return, it will receive technology, construction and operating fees, as well as an undisclosed share of EBITDA after 2030, when the facility is due to start production. All together, GlobalFoundries executives reckon that will amount to $3 billion in cumulative adjusted free cash flow over the first 10 years. A second $11 billion factory is also under consideration, presumably with the same arrangement. It means Japan is bearing all of the risk. Per the wider terms of the 2025 agreement, Tokyo will also share half of available cash flows from the project with the US until it recoups its investment amount plus interest payments, after which 90% of profits will go to the US. Assuming a 5% discount rate, roughly the yield on 30-year US Treasuries, one analysis estimates projects would need to generate annual returns of at least 13% for Japan just to break even, reflecting the large share of profits that go to the US. Washington will also [USN:L6N45Z1AZ TEXT:"more than double"] its stake in GlobalFoundries to 7% as part of the deal, allowing it to capture more of the gains. Hitting that returns hurdle will be hard. GlobalFoundries specialises in churning out commoditised chips used in cars and smartphones. It had an average pre-tax return on invested capital of just 10.4% over the past five years, according to Visible Alpha, far below the roughly 50% at Taiwan's TSMC, which dominates in higher-margin cutting-edge processors. Tokyo can salvage some value elsewhere. The US factory can use Japanese equipment and components, boosting suppliers like Tokyo Electron. Moreover, Renesas, which designs semiconductors for auto giants like Toyota, can also benefit from diversifying manufacturing towards the new GlobalFoundries fabs and away from Taiwan, a democratically ruled island that Beijing claims as its own. And there are worse partners for Tokyo than Abu Dhabi. Perhaps the rich Gulf emirate will ultimately find a way to repay Japan in other ways. Follow Robyn Mak on X . GlobalFoundries on October 15 said it will operate two new semiconductor manufacturing facilities at its New York site. As part of the agreement, Japan will initially invest approximately $10 billion for the first factory that will begin construction by the end of 2026, and potentially another $11 billion in the future. GlobalFoundries, which is owned by Abu Dhabi's sovereign fund Mubadala, will provide technology as well as operating and construction expertise, and receive fees and eventually a share of earnings. The project falls under a US-Japan pact struck last year for Japan to invest $550 billion in the US in return for Washington lowering import trade tariffs. Per the arrangement with the US, Trump selects projects to be funded by Japan. Available free cash flow from investments will be split evenly between the two countries until Japan recoups an agreed-upon amount, after which 90% will go to the US. In a separate agreement, the US Department of Commerce will receive equity in GlobalFoundries of approximately 4%. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Wild's top line likely to test Flames at both ends
item.description: The Minnesota Wild's top line is known for its offense.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Minnesota Wild's top line is known for its offense. Yet the trio of Kirill Kaprizov, Matt Boldy and Joel Eriksson Ek takes at least as much pride in its defense. Their coach thinks it means as much to them to shut down opposing lines as it does to score at the other end of the rink. The star-powered line will look to lead the way again when Minnesota faces the host Calgary Flames on Thursday night. The Wild are coming off one day of rest, while the Flames return to the ice after a three-day break. Kaprizov is the Wild's top threat with 17 points (11 goals, six assists) in 10 games. Quinn Hughes is next with 13 (two goals, 11 assists), Boldy is third with nine (five goals, four assists), and Eriksson Ek rounds out the top four with seven (two goals, five assists). Wild coach John Hynes praised Kaprizov, Boldy and Eriksson Ek for setting the tone at both ends of the ice during the team's hot start to the season. "It's really both," Hynes said. "Those three guys are as good on the offensive side of the puck as they are on the defensive side of the puck. They care about checking and defending. They pay strong attention to detail. ... That's why you respect that line because they play both sides of the puck really hard." Calgary is led by three players with five points apiece through the team's first eight games. The trio includes Morgan Frost (three goals, two assists), Matthew Coronato (two goals, three assists) and Joel Farabee (five assists). The Flames have lost six of their first eight games but are coming off a 3-2 home win over the defending Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday. Calgary coach Ryan Huska said he was encouraged by his team's production against Carolina. During practice this week, he emphasized the importance of getting the puck deep into the offensive zone to set up scoring chances. "A lot of our issues this year have been giving up chances and 'Grade A' chances off the rush," Huska said. "A lot of it is sometimes poor decision (making) with the puck, a turnover higher in the zone or not making your opposing defenseman have to turn and go back to get pucks to wear them down as the night goes on. So, the better we are at that, the more we play in the offensive zone. "There's different ways you can go about doing that. Sometimes it's skating it into the zone. Other times, you're going to have to give it up and put it into an area where you can get it back." Minnesota's options in net include Jesper Wallstedt and Calvin Pickard. Wallstedt is 6-1-2 with a 2.20 goals-against average and a .915 save percentage in nine starts, while Pickard is 0-1-0 with a 5.00 GAA and an .800 save percentage in one start. Calgary could go with Dustin Wolf or Devin Cooley. Wolf is 1-4-0 with a 4.85 GAA and an .834 save percentage in five starts, while Cooley is 1-2-0 with a 4.01 GAA and an .868 save percentage in three starts. Flames captain Mikael Backlund missed practice this week because of an upper-body injury, and his status for Thursday is uncertain. If he cannot play, forward Ben Jones could make his team debut. --Field Level Media

item.title: India bank capital fail is more farce than tragedy
item.description: Sumitomo-backed Yes Bank has been ordered to restore $884 mln of AT1 bonds written off in its 2020 rescue. Their role was a comedy of errors from start to finish. The irony is that the lender's turnaround has made it strong enough to take this latest, painful hit in its stride.
item.dc:creator: Ujjaini Dutta
item.content:encoded: Yes Bank (YESB.NS) is being forced to revisit an existential crisis. Last week India's Supreme Court upheld a ruling ordering the $5.6 billion lender to restore 84 billion rupees ($884 million) of additional Tier 1 capital bonds written off as part of its 2020 collapse. The Reserve Bank of India and the government joined the bank in unsuccessfully appealing the decision. The ruling caps what has been a comedy of errors. The irony is that the lender's turnaround has made it strong enough to take this latest, painful hit in its stride. The rescue itself was necessary and successful. The lender was pushed into administration in March 2020 after bad loans piled up. Authorities stitched together a $1.4 billion bailout led by State Bank of India (SBI.NS) with help from HDFC Bank (HDBK.NS) , ICICI Bank (ICBK.NS) and five others. The lender returned to profitability two years later and until last week's ruling boasted a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio higher than its state-backed rescuer. Yes Bank also bagged a new deep-pocketed shareholder : Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (8316.T) picked up a 25% stake last year. The AT1 bonds case has come back to haunt the bank, though, because of a series of curious flubs at the time. First, the draft turnaround plan explicitly provided for writing them down, but the key bond clause was missing in the final version. Second, India's regulatory framework mandates that AT1 capital be written down before the restructuring process takes effect, not as part of it. And the bank's administrator lacked the authority to wipe them out anyway. Yes Bank's strong comeback at least means reviving the bonds won't kill it. Sure, accounting for the reappearance of the AT1 bonds means its near-11 billion rupee profit in the three months to the end of September would dive to a 52 billion rupee loss. It would also lop 2.3 percentage points off its Common Equity Tier 1 ratio, reducing it to 11.4%, lower than many of its rivals. The prospect of paying the up to 9.5% coupon on the bonds - possibly including accrued interest since 2020 - would sting even more. But the bank is in good enough shape to weather this new storm. Boss Vinay Muralidhar Tonse says that there's no immediate rush to raise capital. And while shareholders wiped some 20%, or $1.4 billion, off the bank's stock market value in the three trading sessions after the ruling, the dip suggests they're concerned only about lost earnings, not a return to a full-blown crisis. That's not the victory the bank was hoping for, but it could have been far worse. Follow Ujjaini Dutta on LinkedIn and X . India's Supreme Court on October 15 set aside Yes Bank's write-off of 84 billion rupees in additional Tier 1 bonds under a restructuring scheme six years ago. The Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation-backed lender’s AT1 bondholders had challenged the write-off, and the Bombay High Court ruled in their favour in 2023. Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India and the federal government appealed that ruling, but the Supreme Court upheld the lower court's decision. The Supreme Court said the bank's administrator did not have the power to write down the bonds after the restructuring scheme was finalised, and ruled that the write-off was "impermissible". The lender on October 17 reported a 65% jump in net profit to 10.80 billion Indian rupees for the September quarter, but said the figure does not reflect the impact of court ruling. Had the impact been recognised, the bank would have posted a quarterly loss of 52.17 billion rupees, it said in a filing. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Epic's 'Fortnite' back on Apple App Store in Australia after antitrust ruling
item.description: Epic Games said its shooter title "Fortnite" will return to Apple's App Store in Australia on Thursday after a federal court ordered the iPhone maker to open up its iOS operating system, having found it violated competition law.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Epic Games said its shooter title "Fortnite" will return to Apple's (AAPL.O) App Store in Australia on Thursday after a federal court ordered the iPhone maker to open up its iOS operating system, having found it violated competition law. Apple said it disagreed with many of the court's findings and would seek to challenge them. "We will request a stay and appeal the outcome to seek a resolution that respects our intellectual property and protects the safe, secure experience that consumers and developers expect from the App Store," an Apple spokesperson told Reuters.

item.title: Tesla aims to sell Cybercab robotaxis by end of year despite federal probe
item.description: Tesla is aiming to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of this year, its engineering chief said on Wednesday, even as the US auto safety agency probes the vehicles that come without manual controls which federal regulations typically require.
item.dc:creator: Abhirup Roy
item.content:encoded: Tesla (TSLA.O) is aiming to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of this year, its engineering chief said on Wednesday, even as the US auto safety agency probes the vehicles that come without manual controls which federal regulations typically require. The gold, two-seaters – that come with butterfly doors and drive themselves without any steering wheel, pedals or mirrors – are one of the key bets CEO Elon Musk has made in his ambition of turning the EV maker into an AI and robotics company. "As Tesla grows, we'll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercabs will be the first," Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering, told analysts after reporting third-quarter results. "We're trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026," he said. "As we start small this year, and we learn ... about delivery and ownership and fleet management of autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we'll continue to scale that." After years of missed promises by Musk, Tesla [USN:L6N44U0OE TEXT:"started offering paid rides"] on a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin, Texas, early last month amid a frenzy of fans and social media influencers. Just hours later, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said it [USN:L4N44V00C TEXT:"opened an investigation"] into Cybercabs to assess how Tesla determined the cars comply with federal vehicle-safety regulations. Those regulations, written decades ago for human-driven vehicles, require manual controls and limit commercial deployment of vehicles that are designed without them. Unlike most other countries, where new vehicle models and technology need regulatory clearance ahead of launch, automakers in the US can deploy them on the public roads by self-certifying that they meet federal standards. NHTSA declined to comment. The agency last month said it was looking into the basis of Tesla's certification of the Cybercab and the extent to which the company determined that certain standards were not applicable to the vehicle. Tesla has until October 30 to respond to the agency. NHTSA has proposed changes to federal safety standards to allow AVs that are designed without human controls. Until those changes are complete, existing standards remain in force, NHTSA has said. SCALING THE CYBERCAB "I think the key thing which we are trying to make sure is that we have all the regulatory approvals where we can start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them," Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's head of AI, said on the call. That aside, "scaling would not be that much of a challenge," he said, adding that the Cybercab was "one of the easiest products" to scale in terms of manufacturing. The Cybercab is part of Tesla's robotaxi network that includes autonomous Model Ys, some with human safety monitors. Over time, Tesla intends to make the Cybercab the main driverless vehicle model operating within a larger robotaxi network. Tesla plans to expand the Cybercab service to Dallas next month, Elluswamy said. The vehicle, however, will mainly be Tesla owned and used for its ride-hailing service, Musk said.

item.title: Amid off-ice drama, Jets focus on ending skid vs. surging Stars
item.description: As the Connor Hellebuyck saga potentially nears a new phase, the Winnipeg Jets remain focused on what they can control on the ice.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: As the Connor Hellebuyck saga potentially nears a new phase, the Winnipeg Jets remain focused on what they can control on the ice. That includes ending their losing streak and an extended skid against the Dallas Stars. With Hellebuyck's team-imposed suspension nearing its end, the visiting Jets will try to avoid a fourth straight loss Thursday night against the surging Stars, who swept all four meetings between the teams last season. An NHL MVP and three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck requested a trade from the Jets before the season and was subsequently suspended by the club for failing to report to training camp. With Winnipeg continuing to explore trade options, a reunion remains possible as the suspension is slated to end Friday, according to multiple media reports. On the ice, the Jets are looking to halt an 0-2-1 skid that has followed their 4-1-1 start. "We have big goals and aspirations for this season, so we know what we want to do," Winnipeg forward Cole Perfetti said. "All that we want is guys that want to be committed to that goal with us." The Jets have lost each of their last three games by one goal, most recently a 2-1 decision at St. Louis on Tuesday. Seven of their nine games have been decided by one goal. Winnipeg has scored just three goals over its last two contests. "Greasy goals, the stuff around the net front, get yourself into those hard areas," Jets coach Scott Arniel said. "Those are things you have to work on all the time." Winnipeg's Stuart Skinner made 26 saves against St. Louis and is 3-1-2 with a 2.65 goals-against average. Teammate Clay Stevenson has allowed nine goals while going 1-2-0 in three starts. The Jets surrendered 16 goals while going 0-3-1 against the Stars last season. Dallas has outscored its opponents 10-4 during a three-game winning streak, including a 3-2 overtime victory over the visiting Boston Bruins on Tuesday. Mikko Rantanen recorded a hat trick, with Jason Robertson assisting on two of his goals. Rantanen has 11 points (five goals, six assists) through nine games. "He's just a beast," linemate Wyatt Johnston said of Rantanen. "He's very special and can do things that not many other guys can do." Rantanen recorded nine points (two goals, seven assists) in four games against Winnipeg last season. After stopping 18 of 20 shots Tuesday, Dallas goaltender Jake Oettinger is 4-2-1 with a 1.13 GAA and .945 save percentage through seven starts. Backup Casey DeSmith has allowed a pair of goals in each of his first two starts. After being held scoreless in the season's first two games, Robertson has totaled nine points (three goals, six assists) over his last seven. He scored three goals against the Jets last season. Meanwhile, Perfetti scored his sixth goal of the season Tuesday. He recorded three points in three games against Dallas last season. Teammate Kyle Connor leads Winnipeg with 11 points, including eight goals, but has been held off the scoresheet in the last two games. He has recorded 35 points in 33 career games against Dallas. --Field Level Media

item.title: Indonesia issues record fines to companies over stock market violations
item.description: Indonesia's financial regulator has handed over sanction letters to parties found to have violated trading rules in three listed companies, with fines totalling 2.1 trillion rupiah ($116.67 million), it said late on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indonesia's financial regulator has handed over sanction letters to parties found to have violated trading rules in three listed companies, with fines totalling 2.1 trillion rupiah ($116.67 million), it said late on Wednesday. The fines, linked to trading in PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk (DSSA.JK) , PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk <BREN.JK> and PT Petrindo Jaya Kreasi Tbk <CUAN.JK>, were the biggest the regulator, known by its Indonesian abbreviation OJK, has ever imposed, its chair Friderica Widyasari Dewi told reporters. The OJK only identified the sanctioned parties by their initials The [USN:L6N4620JP TEXT:"penalties"] were part of capital market reforms, OJK said last week, after MSCI [USN:L4N46124S TEXT:"warned"] it could demote Indonesian equities from "emerging" to "standalone" market status because not enough was being done to combat coordinated trading practices in its stock market OJK said it imposed a 1.5 trillion rupiah ($83.33 million) fine on a company identified as SMT for market manipulation of Dian Swastatika's shares that led to a sharp jump in the price Dian Swastatika is part of Indonesian conglomerate Sinar Mas group and operates in mining and energy A company identified as AH Ltd was fined 500 billion rupiah for obfuscating information during the initial public offering of geothermal company Barito Renewables, while TC Pte Ltd was fined 100 billion rupiah for a similar offence related to the IPO of energy and mineral firm Petrindo, OJK said Parties affiliated with the controlling shareholders of Barito Renewables and Petrindo were found to have concealed their affiliations and received a large portion of shares ahead of their respective IPOs, limiting the number of shares available on the market, the regulator said Barito Renewables and Petrindo are both controlled by Indonesian tycoon Prajogo Pangestu Those fined, Sinar Mas Group and Pangestu could not immediately be reached for comment The regulator announced the fines on Friday but did not go into detail. Dian Swastatika, Barito Renewables and Petrindo separately said in stock exchange filings on Monday that they respected the OJK's law enforcement measures and would follow the rules The three companies were part of MSCI's indices but were [USN:L1N41Q01N TEXT:"removed"] earlier this year OJK also said it fined several securities companies over stock market violations and temporarily froze underwriting permits for two individuals. It identified the fined parties only by their initials ($1 = 18,000.0000 rupiah)

item.title: Bank of Korea holds rates, upbeat outlook points to future hikes
item.description: The Bank of Korea kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country's export momentum.
item.dc:creator: Cynthia Kim, Jihoon Lee
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Korea kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country's export momentum. The seven-member monetary policy board at the BOK voted to keep the seven-day repurchase rate (KROCRT=ECI) at 3.00%, a decision that was [USN:L6N46505J TEXT:"forecast"] by all 34 analysts surveyed by Reuters. The central bank said that further tightening remains on the table, stating it "will decide the timing and pace of future increases" while assessing inflation, financial stability and domestic economic trends. "The growth rates for this year and next year are expected to be considerably higher than the August forecasts of 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively," the BOK said in a statement, adding a pause on Thursday was needed to evaluate external risks and the lagging effects of its back-to-back hikes in July and August. It also said that both headline and core inflation for next year will exceed previous forecasts. OPEN-MINDED ON NEXT HIKE During a news conference, BOK Governor Shin Hyun Song declined to comment on a question about terminal interest rates and added "I don’t believe it is necessary to strictly follow that path (market consensus)." Instead of sticking to a fixed trajectory, Shin said the bank will evaluate incoming data as it emerges. "We will refine our own thinking and continue to conduct monetary policy with an open mind," he added. Analyst consensus puts the peak policy rate at 3.50%, pricing in one more hike this November and another in the first quarter of 2027. "His statement that the bank won't blindly follow market estimates shouldn't be interpreted as casting doubt on a 3.50% terminal rate - rather, it suggests the actual path could differ from the projected November and Q1 timeline," said Paik Yoon-min, analyst at Kyobo Securities. "Passing on a November hike carries risks, as moving forward with it is crucial to signal a firm stance on containing inflation." Paik sees the BOK raising interest rates at its November 26 meeting and in the first quarter of 2027. Three-year bond futures held steady as the market largely anticipated that the BOK would signal another rate hike, potentially in November. The US Federal Reserve target rate sits at 4.00% following a 25-basis-point hike in September. The current market consensus expects the Fed to hold rates steady at its October meeting before implementing a final year-end hike in December. For the BOK, the July and August increases were its first consecutive hikes in more than three years, after which Shin said a gradual pace of tightening was preferred. Shin, however, reiterated at an International Monetary Fund event on October 13 that policy would remain restrictive until inflation converges to its target. Headline consumer inflation slowed to 2.9% in September from 3.1% in August, remaining above the bank's 2% target. [USN:L1N45N002 TEXT:"Exports"] are powering ahead thanks to global spending on artificial intelligence. Shipments from January to September topped $800 billion for the first time ever.

item.title: Meta sued in Australian class action over alleged social media harm to children
item.description: A class-action lawsuit has been filed in an Australian court against Meta Platforms' Facebook and Instagram that alleges the social media platforms exposed children to harmful content and kept them addicted through algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A class-action lawsuit has been filed in an Australian court against Meta Platforms' (META.O) Facebook and Instagram that alleges the social media platforms exposed children to harmful content and kept them addicted through algorithms. The lawsuit, filed in the Federal Court, Australia's second-highest, by law firm MinterEllison this month could be the first in Australia to blame social media for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers. The class-action suit has been filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs, who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were under the age of 18, and are seeking compensation. "We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously," a Meta spokesperson said by email. In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information which could reveal the identity of the applicants, and the statement of claim. The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech after a [USN:L1N3XF0HL TEXT:"world-first"] ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off [USN:L1N45003L TEXT:"algorithm-driven"] content on their feeds. Meta in August [USN:L6N44N0VA TEXT:"agreed"] to pay $18 billion to settle with nearly all US states to resolve claims it designed social media to addict children.

item.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange strikes as US envoy leaves after talks
item.description: Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, a Reuters witness said, and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight, as the two sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US mediation attempts to end the war.
item.dc:creator: Gleb Garanich, Jekaterina Golubkova
item.content:encoded: Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, a Reuters witness said, and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight, as the two sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US mediation attempts to end the war. The Russian strikes wounded 15 people and [USN:P8N44K019 TEXT:"damaged"] subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in the Ukrainian capital while also restricting traffic there, Kyiv authorities said. The strikes followed another attack on the city [USN:L1N46711S TEXT:"on Wednesday evening"] that wounded six people. A Russian strike killed a woman and injured another four people in the Kharkiv region in Ukraine's northeast, Regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram. A drone also [USN:P8N44K01B TEXT:"hit"] energy infrastructure in the Kremenchuk area in the Poltava region, a local official said on Telegram, without giving details. Located on the Dnipro River, Kremenchuk is a major industrial hub and home to one of Ukraine's biggest oil refineries. The area has been repeatedly hit by Russian strikes, including a 2022 attack on a crowded shopping mall that killed at least 21 people. In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow after 630 drones were sent towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin [USN:P8N44K018 TEXT:"said"] on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added. In the city of Lipetsk - home to a major steel plant some 400 km (250 miles) south of Moscow - a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on the Telegram app. Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 after annexing the Crimea peninsula from its southern neighbour eight years earlier, locking the two nations into the deadliest conflict on the European continent since World War Two. The latest strikes come after US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff [USN:L1N4670ZQ TEXT:"held"] talks this week with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russia's President Vladimir Putin to mediate an end to the conflict. Zelenskiy [USN:L1N4670ZQ TEXT:"said"] on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for three-way talks with Russia and the United States at the level of negotiators to be held as soon as possible, and the Kremlin [USN:L6N4670P2 TEXT:"said"] Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month.

item.title: BHP chair points to Canada tax incentives in call for investment reforms
item.description: Australia must pay close attention to tax incentives and business-friendly measures offered by countries such as Canada if it wants to compete more effectively for global investment, BHP Chair Ross McEwan said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia must pay close attention to tax incentives and business-friendly measures offered by countries such as Canada if it wants to compete more effectively for global investment, BHP (BHP.AX) Chair Ross McEwan said on Thursday. Speaking at BHP's annual general meeting, McEwan said, "Make no mistake, Australia must compete for capital if it wants to win – nationally, and in every state." Canada had recently announced a "Productivity Mega Deduction", allowing businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of eligible capital investments, he said, adding that the country also allows miners to fully deduct mine development costs in the year they are incurred. Such measures lower the tax burden on new investments, improve returns and give companies greater confidence to commit capital, McEwan said, describing Canada's approach as a practical example of how government policy can boost productivity and attract investment. He said similar examples could be found in other countries where miner BHP invests, including Argentina and Chile. "Australia should pay close attention to that." BHP will face an investor campaign over the next year to set a 2040 emissions reduction target, ACCR Chief Executive Brynn O'Brien said at the AGM. BHP aims to cut its operational greenhouse gas emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030 and has a longer-term goal of reaching net zero by 2050. O'Brien urged the company to commit to setting a 2040 target within the next year, but McEwan declined, saying BHP was focused on advancing growth projects and reducing its reliance on diesel. [USN:P8N3PI05C TEXT:"McEwan also said"] there would come a time when BHP will take a more serious look at uranium, but for now the market remained "too small" for the miner to pursue as a core commodity. "There'll be a time when we'll have a look at that and say, is that commodity big enough for us to be involved in it as an asset that we are focusing on? At this stage, the answer to that is still no," he said. BHP currently produces around 5% of global uranium supply from its South Australian operations.

item.title: From groceries to home loans, high oil prices permeate daily life
item.description: The shock of oil prices at a five-month high of $110 a barrel and gas prices in Asia and Europe hitting their highest levels since December 2022 is making its mark on household budgets.
item.dc:creator: Seher Dareen, Anushree Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: The shock of oil prices at a five-month high of $110 a barrel and gas prices in [USN:L8N4650OY TEXT:"Asia"] and [USN:L1N4660F0 TEXT:"Europe"] hitting their highest levels since December 2022 is making its mark on household budgets. As well as raising the costs of transport and heating, it adds to pressure on food, clothing and packaging prices and contributes to elevated levels of inflation and borrowing costs. The following graphics illustrate some of the ways in which the rally is having an impact on daily life around the world. The Iran war has already pushed global diesel prices to record highs. Average [USN:L8N45O0OV TEXT:"British"] diesel pump prices hit £2.00 ($2.64) per litre for the first time this month and US prices hit a record of $6.53 a gallon in September. In response, US President Donald Trump has allowed [USN:L1N45R0NK TEXT:"red-dyed diesel"], which is used in equipment and vehicles that are not usually operated on public roadways and is exempt from highway taxes, to be accessed by anyone until the end of the year. The impact extends to mortgage rates as energy prices contribute to rising inflation, which major central banks are attempting to rein in by raising interest rates. [USN:L8N46708O TEXT:"British inflation"] and borrowing rose more than expected last month. The increase in August, which the Office for National Statistics said was due to higher petrol and diesel costs, took inflation to its highest since October 2025. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate to a 15-year high last month, leading the country's mostly variable housing loan rates to rise in tandem, weighing on [USN:L1N45M19O TEXT:"home prices"]. When buying a house with an average loan of A$731,000 ($513,966) on a 30-year mortgage, a rise in interest rates from 5.5% in 2025 to 6.2% now raises annual repayments by around A$3,900 ($2,742). Meanwhile in the United States, mortgage purchase activity has weakened as 30-year mortgage rates climbed from around 6.1% to about 7.5%, increasing borrowing costs for prospective homebuyers. Most people opt for fixed rates. Other parts of household budgets also suffer, particularly those relying on heating oil for winter. In the state of New York, heating bills will likely rise by 47% from last year, National Energy Assistance Directors Association data shows. In Britain, where gas is the main fuel used for heating, households could see a 10% year-on-year rise in bills this quarter, EnergyUK estimates. Since most plastics are made from oil or natural gas and then converted into polymers for making everything from bottles to sneakers, as well as polyester fabric for clothing, the increase in crude prices is having a wider effect. For common grocery items, packaging of any type, whether plastic, paper or glass, typically represents 5% to 15% of a product's manufacturing cost, according to consultancy MAT . US plastic prices rose 7% in August versus October 2025. In the US, [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"consumer prices"] accelerated in September, with a surge in gasoline prices accounting for more than half of the rise. Global [USN:L4N45Z033 TEXT:"food inflation"] is poised to accelerate further and persist well into 2027 on shipping disruptions and higher costs for fertiliser, which is also made from natural gas, data from the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization showed. ($1 = 1.4223 Australian dollars)

item.title: Australia's CSL faces shareholder class action over forecast disclosures
item.description: Australian biotech firm CSL said on Thursday it is facing a shareholder class action in Victoria's Supreme Court over claims it breached continuous disclosure rules tied to its financial forecasts, sending its shares lower.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australian biotech firm CSL (CSL.AX) said on Thursday it is facing a shareholder class action in Victoria's Supreme Court over claims it breached continuous disclosure rules tied to its financial forecasts, sending its shares lower. The legal action marks the latest challenge for CSL after a string of profit warnings, a delayed Seqirus demerger and a $5 billion impairment charge rattled investors and wiped billions from its market value over 2025 and 2026. The class action was filed by law firm Echo Law on behalf of investors who acquired certain CSL securities between February 11, 2025, and May 11, 2026. "The allegations relate to the company's medium-term and FY26 guidance, both of which were retracted or downgraded during the claim period, and the reasonableness of the guidance in the context of changes to market conditions for immunoglobulin and albumin products in 2024 and 2025," Echo Law said in a statement on its website. Denying any liability, CSL said it had been in compliance with its disclosure obligations at all times, adding that it would defend the proceeding. Shares of CSL fell as much as 1.1% to A$193.89 by 0022 GMT, cutting its year-to-date gains to around 13%. CSL cut its forecast for fiscal 2026 revenue and net profit after tax before amortisation at its [USN:L4N3W81P2 TEXT:"annual general meeting"] in late October 2025. It also delayed plans to spin off its Seqirus vaccine unit, blaming an unprecedented fall in US flu immunisation rates. At the 2025 annual meeting, about 42% of proxy votes were cast against CSL's remuneration report, according to a tally shown that day, underscoring investor frustration after a steep share-price fall. In [USN:L1N41N067 TEXT:"May this year"], CSL warned of a $5 billion impairment and cut its 2026 revenue forecast to $15.2 billion on a constant-currency basis, reigniting doubts about the merits of its Vifor acquisition and the pace of its turnaround. On Wednesday, CSL [USN:L4N4670C7 TEXT:"named"] GSK (GSK.L) executive Deborah Waterhouse as its next CEO and managing director, effective February.

item.title: New World screwworm cases confirmed in wildlife in Texas, beef cow in New Mexico
item.description: The US Department of Agriculture said on Wednesday it confirmed the first detection of flesh-eating parasite New World screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Pecos County, Texas, while New Mexico authorities separately said they confirmed a case in a beef cow.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: The US Department of Agriculture said on Wednesday it confirmed the first detection of flesh-eating parasite New World screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Pecos County, Texas, while New Mexico authorities separately said they confirmed a case in a beef cow. The elk was located on a game ranch and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA said in a statement. The Texas Animal Health Commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department are conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said. The New Mexico Department of Agriculture said later that animal health officials confirmed a case of New World screwworm in a beef cow in the state's Otero County. New Mexico authorities said state and federal officials were continuing to expand surveillance and fly-trapping around affected locations to identify any additional cases and determine whether the pest had spread beyond the affected animals. Officials have established a minimum 12.4-mile (20 km) radius infested zone around the affected animal's location, the New Mexico Department of Agriculture said. Within this zone, animals must be inspected and, if necessary, treated before moving within or out of the area, state authorities added. Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports. The US [USN:L1N45912W TEXT:"halted livestock"] imports from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm but resumed trade in August at an Arizona port as part of a phased reopening plan. The halt tightened US cattle supplies, contributing to a rise in beef prices to record highs for American consumers.

item.title: STRICTLY EMBARGOED UNTIL WEDS 11PM - U.S. climate champion Gina McCarthy honoured in Reuters Global Sustainability awards
item.description: Gina McCarthy seems remarkably chipper given the seemingly relentless opposition to climate action, led by her own government under President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Balch
item.content:encoded: Gina McCarthy seems remarkably chipper given the seemingly relentless opposition to climate action, led by her own government under President Donald Trump. McCarthy, who was head of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Obama administration, and White House climate adviser under Joe Biden, accepts that her view isn’t universally held. “It may sound a little crazy to people,” she says. “But I'm really bullish on what's happening next.” She spoke to The Ethical Corporation on the eve of Reuters Global Sustainability Awards, where she was honoured with a Lifetime Achievement award, in recognition of spending more than three decades “at the forefront of America's fight for cleaner air, safer water, and a liveable climate”. Her bullishness was also clear in her acceptance speech, which was delivered by video from her home outside Boston. “Despite all the nonsense from my federal government and their fossil fuel allies, there has been a massive surge this past year in clean energy,” she said, with state and local governments from across the U.S. “working together to drive a more aggressive energy transition ... with a relentless spirit of optimism”. McCarthy will be taking that optimistic spirit to next month’s United Nations’ climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, as chair of America Is All In , a coalition of pro-climate U.S. cities, states, corporations and community groups. Newly assembled solar panels at a new solar facility in Humble, Texas, US, October 6, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian “We don't want the rest of the world to think that the United States is what Trump says. The United States is what our state and local governments say,” she tells The Ethical Corporation. With the U.S. midterm elections, in the week prior to COP31, expected to restore the House of Representatives to Democratic control and weaken Republicans’ grip on the Senate, that message will be even easier to sell. She cites Illinois, which has passed legislation to add 3 gigawatts of battery storage to its grid by 2030, and California, which plans to modernise its already pioneering carbon credit programme. Cleveland, Ohio, meanwhile, is pursuing a new five-year plan to cut emissions by nearly two-thirds (against 2018 levels). Sceptics will note that all the examples derive from strongly Democrat-controlled constituencies, but McCarthy points out that the Republican stronghold of Texas is home to a substantial portion of the record additions of solar and battery projects added to the U.S. grid in the past year. McCarthy has long believed that for the average U.S. voter, economics trump ideology when it comes to powering their homes and businesses. A drone view shows California’s largest battery storage facility, as it nears completion on a 43-acre site in Menifee, California, U.S., March 28, 2024. REUTERS/Mike Blake The relative affordability of renewable power compared to fossil fuels makes it increasingly attractive to householders, in the face of a monthly inflation rate of 3.4%. Corporations, meanwhile, have been leaning heavily into renewable energy, mindful not only of rising energy costs but growing threats to energy security. According to the business-backed Corporate Energy Buyers Association (CEBA), corporate-sponsored clean energy projects in 2025 exceeded the total power generation of 45 individual U.S. states. With U.S. investment in the global clean energy transition now running at around $378 billion, it may seem like supporters of America Is All In, who collectively represent 63% of the U.S. population and 74% of U.S. GDP, can rest easy. Gina McCarthy pictured in Washington in 2014 as she arrives to sign a proposal under the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution from existing power plants. REUTERS/Joshua Roberts Yet having seen many of the environmental advances made under her watch rolled back by the Trump Administration, McCarthy is far from complacent. In mid-September, for example, the EPA, which she headed up between 2013 and 2017, said it planned to desist from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector. According to America Is All In, the proposed move could see a potential ten-fold increase in coal-fired power, with severe impacts on greenhouse gas emissions but also human health. “To have this (Clean Power Plan) arbitrarily taken off the books by this administration was absolutely ludicrous. It had nothing but benefits,” she says. Another policy reversal that she admits was “not easy” to watch was the scrapping of the EPA’s landmark 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding , barring the agency from tracking and capping emissions from cars and heavy-duty vehicles. But it was the dilution of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) that McCarthy deems the most consequential of all the Trump administration’s recent moves to halt transition efforts. Introduced in the wake of the COVID pandemic, the IRA earmarked around $485 billion in public spending and tax breaks for investments in healthcare, clean tech and other transition-related investments. Its dismantlement continues to incense McCarthy, who describes it as “one of the biggest opportunities that our country ever had” to provide U.S. citizens with clean, secure and affordable energy. A drone view shows Elon Musk's xAI Colossus 2 "Macrohard" data centre in Southaven, Mississippi, U.S., May 30, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Wurm Yet her response is typically indefatigable. “You know, we all have to pull up our big boy, big girl pants when these challenges happen.” Fuelling her confidence are two fundamental convictions; namely, that people will be ultimately won over by clean power’s cost competitiveness, and will also realise that “this administration isn’t forever”. She takes heart from the multiple lawsuits now being brought by state authorities and campaign groups against various efforts by the Trump administration to weaken environmental protections. Earlier this month, a coalition of 25 cities and states – including New York, California, North Carolina and Washington D.C. – issued a petition to the U.S. court of appeals for the District of Columbia to review the EPA’s proposal to remove emission standards for power plants. Also encouraging is the spirit of cross-sector collaboration that is now emerging across the U.S. She points to the C40 Global Urban Data Centres Pact . A new mayor-led initiative endorsed by 49 cities, including 22 in the U.S., seeks to promote greater public accountability in the management of resource-hungry data centres. The pact, which includes Chicago, Austin, Seattle and Miami, comes on the back of increasing disquiet in the U.S. over the water and energy consumption of AI data centres. While McCarthy acknowledges the potential economic benefits of such facilities, she argues that companies and regulators have not paid enough attention at their environmental and community impacts. She would like to see tax revenues from data centres used to help fund renewable energy projects and community infrastructure. “They (data centres) are one of the fastest-growing challenges that we have in the United States,” she says. “There has to be a way to ensure that they can do their thing without destroying us.” Reuters Events Global Sustainability Awards 2026: other winners AI for Sustainability Excellence Award — Winner : Tracera; Highly Commended : Jupiter Intelligence Biodiversity Champion Award — Winner: Olam Agri; Highly Commended : Rainforest Expeditions Business Transformation Award — Winner : Pure Data Centres Group; Highly Commende d: Pandora Circularity Award — Winner : LIXIL Corporation; Highly Commended : Groupe SEB Data-driven Sustainability Communication Award — Winner : Syngenta Group; Highly Commended : Diversified Energy Company Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Award — Winner : Atlas Renewable Energy; Highly Commended : Halkbank Leadership in Water Stewardship Award — Winner : SPG Dry Cooling; Highly Commended : Nestle Waters & Premium Beverages Net Zero: Leadership Award — Winner : Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited; Highly Commended : Edison International Net Zero: Operations Transformation Award — Winner : Cushman & Wakefield and Standard Chartered; Highly Commended : Bodycote plc Net Zero: Supply Chain Decarbonisation Award — Winner : Schneider Electric; Highly Commended : AstraZeneca Partnership of the Year Award — Winner : Hindustan Unilever Limited; Highly Commended : Aviva Product Innovation Award — Winner : Hitachi Energy; Highly Commended : Fairphone Responsible Investor of the Year Award — Winner : Circulate Capital; Highly Commended : EFG Holding Rising Sustainability Star Award — Winner : Daniel Kopp; Highly Commended: Marine Sanouiller SDG Pioneer of the Year Award — Winner : Telkom Indonesia; Highly Commended : Sunbeth Global Concepts Ltd.
