item.content:encoded: Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz hat vor mittlerweile täglichen hybriden Angriffen Russlands auf Deutschland gewarnt und gleichzeitig eine Kapitulation der Ukraine abgelehnt. "Meine größte Sorge ist im Moment nicht unsere Wirtschaft, nicht die Europäische Union, nicht Amerika und nicht China", sagte Merz am Mittwoch beim Berlin Global Dialogue (BGD). "Meine größte Sorge sind die Auswirkungen Russlands auf unsere Gesellschaft und die Art und Weise, wie es ihnen gelingt, unsere Gesellschaften zu destabilisieren." Man erlebe permanent Angriffe Russlands und müsse widerstandsfähig werden. Die fortwährenden Desinformationen aus Moskau würden auch noch von einer Partei geschürt, sagte er in Anspielung auf die AfD. Deshalb sei auch klar, warum Deutschland die Ukraine weiter in ihrem Abwehrkampf gegen den russischen Angreifer unterstütze. "Das ist nicht nur ein Krieg in der Ukraine. Das ist ein grundlegender Angriff auf die gesamte politische Ordnung, die wir nach 1990 erreicht haben", sagte er. Mit Blick auf die neuen Russland-Avancen von US-Präsident Donald Trump fügte der Kanzler hinzu: "Eine Kapitulation – oder gar eine bedingungslose Kapitulation der Ukraine – kommt nicht infrage. Denn das wäre eine Kapitulation von uns allen." Deutschland und die Europäer unterstützten die Ukraine im eigenen Interesse. Regierungssprecher Stefan Kornelius bestätigte, dass der außen- und sicherheitspolitische Berater des Kanzlers bei den Gesprächen in Oslo zwischen dem US-Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff, dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj, dem norwegischen Ministerpräsidenten Jonas Gahr Støre und dem finnischen Präsidenten Alexander Stubb anwesend gewesen sei. Für die Bundesregierung sei klar, dass es keine Vereinbarung über die Köpfe der Ukraine und der Europäer hinweg geben könne.

item.title: Apple will have limited iPhone Duo units available in stores on Friday
item.description: Apple on Wednesday said it will have 'limited' numbers of its folding iPhone Duo phone available for walk-in customers when the device launches Friday, after initial online orders sold out in minutes and pushed delivery times for some customers to January.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis
item.content:encoded: Apple (AAPL.O) on Wednesday said it will have 'limited' numbers of its folding iPhone Duo phone available for walk-in customers when the device launches Friday, after initial online orders sold out in minutes and pushed delivery times for some customers to January. Apple announced its first folding phone in September, with analysts expecting it to quickly come to dominate a niche segment where rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for years. But the iPhone Duo is also a more complex product than standard candy-bar iPhones, with a tight-fitting hinge that analysts believe may take time for Apple to learn to manufacture in high volumes. “On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," Apple said in a statement. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible.” The availability of walk-in units will vary by country, Apple said. Online order pickup and limited walk-in purchases will be available in the United States, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of the UK and Europe. But other regions will only have iPhone Duo units available for customers who already bought them online. Those include mainland China, France, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the UAE, Apple said. In the China-governed territory of Macau, the iPhone Duo will be available for walk-in customers only, with limited inventory, Apple said. (This story has been refiled to clarify that Macau is a territory of China, in paragraph 7 . )

item.title: Israel's election may change its leader, but not Iran war policy
item.description: Israel's election next week may change its leader, but not its strategy: Iran will remain its chief adversary, military force will continue to be its preferred tool and Palestinian statehood a distant prospect, regional policymakers and analysts say.
item.dc:creator: Samia Nakhoul
item.content:encoded: Israel's election next week may change its leader, but not its strategy: Iran will remain its chief adversary, military force will continue to be its preferred tool and Palestinian statehood a distant prospect, regional policymakers and analysts say. That is because the strategic assumptions underpinning Israeli policy were hardened by the October 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israeli communities by Palestinian militant group Hamas and by the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. If anything, Israel could toughen its security policy, the analysts said, as victory for Prime Minister [USN:L1N45L0EX TEXT:"Benjamin Netanyahu"] with the backing of [USN:L1N46608F TEXT:"far-right"] coalition partners could embolden him to step up the war with Iran, tighten Israel's grip on the occupied West Bank and push diplomacy further to the margins. Israel's security doctrine now rests on three pillars: breaking Iran, holding buffer zones beyond its borders and using force to deter enemies. The real divide is one of degree rather than direction — how aggressively Israel fights its wars, how far it expands Jewish [USN:L1N464047 TEXT:"settlements in the West Bank"] and whether any leader opts for diplomacy, the analysts said. From Tehran to Riyadh, [USN:L8N3XX04M TEXT:"Tuesday's election"] is not seen as a potential turning point but as a test of whether the Middle East is settling into a long confrontation, where wars ebb and flow while the underlying conflicts are unresolved. "If Netanyahu is elected, he'll do whatever he thinks he wants to do," said Aviv Bushinsky, a former adviser to Netanyahu. "Expansion of the settlements will continue. The wars against Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah will continue." "What you see now is what you'll see after the election, maybe even more aggressively," he said. "As long as Iran is in such a situation, it's a waste of time talking about Palestine.” Netanyahu said on Sunday that Israel must prioritise “prevention and offence over containment and defence”, including pre-emptive strikes to thwart emerging threats, while establishing Israel as a regional power and maximising its independence in armaments. WHY THE COURSE IS UNLIKELY TO CHANGE The election pits Netanyahu's right-wing Likud and its ultranationalist allies against an opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party. Palestinian analyst Ghassan al-Khatib sees no prospect of a fundamental shift in policy towards the Palestinians, with Israeli political parties competing to project harder-line positions as public opinion moves further to the right. “The substance of the policy remains the same: No to a Palestinian state and yes to further settlement expansion. On this, they are all in agreement,” he said. A government led by Netanyahu's opponents might seek to repair Israel's international standing by curbing some settler violence or pursuing settlement expansion with less fanfare. But such changes would be a shift in style rather than substance, al-Khatib said. In response to Reuters questions on Iran and the West Bank, a State Department spokesperson said Washington would continue to pressure Tehran "as long as Iran devotes its energy revenues to financing attacks on our allies, supporting terrorism around the world, and pursuing other destabilizing actions, we will use all the tools at our disposal to hold the regime accountable." The spokesperson also said the  United States did not support Israel annexing the West Bank. "A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region," they said. Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Center said Israel's security establishment and much of its political class share a common strategic outlook, centred on confronting Iran, maintaining "forward defence" and preserving military deterrence, reducing the scope for big policy shifts. Joost Hiltermann of the International Crisis Group, who has conducted research in the West Bank, said growing settler violence, mounting Palestinian frustration and the absence of a "political horizon" had created combustible conditions, where even a minor trigger could spark a wider uprising. 'VENOMOUS OCTOPUS' Some regional policymakers ask whether Israel's confrontation with Iran has become the organising principle of Middle East security, regardless of who wins the election. US President [USN:L1N46403J TEXT:"Donald Trump's"] praise of Netanyahu as a "great warrior prime minister" has reinforced expectations that the Israeli leader will try to finish the campaign against Tehran if he retains power. Netanyahu has made clear his ambitions extend beyond containing Iran to toppling its clerical rulers. "There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all: overthrow the regime in Iran," he said at a military officer graduation ceremony on Wednesday, adding it was his directive to the military, Mossad and other security agencies. “Completing the task means toppling the terrorist regime in Iran, the head of the venomous octopus,” he said in another speech this week. But military and political analysts question whether anything short of a US-Israeli ground invasion would force Tehran to abandon what it views as its core security interests in what it sees as an existential fight. After surviving months of war, Iran may be betting it can outlast its opponents while continuing to exert pressure through regional allies. "This is a quagmire," Young said. "The Iranians can outlast Trump." Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza have been weakened, but the broader network of Iran-aligned groups has survived and the conflict could strengthen Tehran's determination to pursue a nuclear deterrent, the analysts said. For all the alarm Netanyahu causes in the Arab world, some Gulf leaders still see him as the Israeli politician most likely to keep Iran under pressure. This creates a dilemma for them. They oppose what they view as his expansionist policies but want Iranian influence curbed. "Netanyahu's policies in Gaza, the West Bank, Syria and Lebanon are damaging," said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Center. "As for Iran, a settlement is needed before the conflict escalates further. If Iran's role is not curbed, the region could be heading toward 50 years of Iranian hegemony."

item.title: Nigeria reports Ebola case as outbreak reaches West Africa
item.description: Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in more than a decade on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that health officials have described as the fastest-spreading on record.
item.dc:creator: Elisha Bala-Gbogbo, Camillus Eboh
item.content:encoded: Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in more than a decade on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that health officials have described as the [USN:L6N4421DF TEXT:"fastest-spreading on record"]. The Ebola species behind the outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine. Since the first cases were confirmed in Democratic Republic of Congo in May, the disease has killed 4,646 people. Health officials fear misinformation and [USN:L8N45M12L TEXT:"funding shortfalls"] could fuel further spread within the region and across borders. Cases have also been reported in Uganda and, more recently, Kenya. "Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa. The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level," Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Jean Kaseya said on X on Wednesday. The Nigerian case involves a Ugandan woman who arrived in Nigeria's capital Abuja via Addis Ababa on October 5, Odianosen Ehiakhamen of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control told Arise TV on Tuesday. She began feeling unwell two days later and sought treatment at a private hospital in Abuja on October 11 with malaria-like symptoms, but her condition did not improve, Ehiakhamen said. CONCERN OF 'PAN-AFRICAN EVENT' After health officials learned she had recently travelled to Uganda, one of the countries affected by the current outbreak, they tested her for Ebola on October 19. The positive result was confirmed on Tuesday. "My concern, now that this has spread from East Africa to West Africa, is that we now have a pan-African event, as opposed to a few at-risk countries," said Ayoade Alakija, a Nigerian physician who co-chairs a G7 committee for investment in global health. Alakija also noted that it had taken 12 days since the woman fell sick for her to be tested for Ebola, potentially exposing many other people to the infection. "Abuja is one of Africa's main cities ... with air and road connections daily, multiple, across the world. It’s a very different prospect – and that's what worries me — the amount of time it took." Nigerian authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them healthcare workers. They include the patient's husband, a Swiss national who lives with her in Abuja. Officials are also tracing passengers who travelled with her from Uganda to Nigeria but do not believe she was symptomatic during the flight. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving treatment. UGANDA SAYS IT HAS NO ACTIVE EBOLA CASES Uganda's health ministry said the woman had travelled to Congo, where more than 9,500 Ebola cases have been recorded across eight provinces. It was not immediately clear where she had been in Congo, and Nigerian authorities have not confirmed that she had visited the country. "Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here," Uganda's health ministry said, adding that the country has no active Ebola cases. Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country [USN:L6N44N0VL TEXT:"Ebola-free"] in August. Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, involving a traveller who arrived from Congo via Uganda. The country has since reported [USN:L1N4660OP TEXT:"nine cases"], all linked to the same patient. The spread of Ebola to Kenya raised questions about the effectiveness of [USN:L6N45S157 TEXT:"border screening systems"] designed to prevent cross-border transmission. Pate, Nigeria's health minister, said the country had successfully contained Ebola in 2014 during the West African epidemic, the largest outbreak on record. He said Nigeria had the systems in place to respond to the new case.

item.title: Wall St sees Tesla-SpaceX merger as inevitable, but split on price
item.description: A Tesla-SpaceX merger appears to be a matter of when, not if, to many on Wall Street. But they disagree on a key factor: how much Tesla shareholders should be paid.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram
item.content:encoded: A Tesla-SpaceX merger appears to be a matter of when, not if, to many on Wall Street. But they disagree on a key factor: how much Tesla shareholders should be paid. That tension runs through [USN:L4N4661M0 TEXT:"a deal"] where predictions on the premium Tesla shareholders would get to swap into a stock of SpaceX (SPCX.O) that Elon Musk controls run from little or none to 35%. With Tesla (TSLA.O) worth about $1.5 trillion, the premium could run into hundreds of billions of dollars, making it a major swing factor in any deal. The billionaire, a self-described 'conflicted party', said the committees are [USN:L1N46701K TEXT:"yet to agree"] on terms, even as Wall Street sees a deal being proposed in the coming months. Tesla shares gained more than 3%, while SpaceX rose 11% on Wednesday and was set to add about $210 billion to its market capitalization if gains hold, roughly equal to that of CitiGroup (C.N) . SpaceX and Tesla are jointly developing the Terafab chip plant, and AI now makes up more than half of SpaceX's revenue, with another $35 billion to $40 billion spending likely in fourth quarter to fund further expansion. "(A Tesla-SpaceX merger) is very strategic as both companies are [USN:L6N43O1D8 TEXT:"rapidly transitioning"] into artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and both have huge infrastructure projects underway," said Justus Parmar, CEO of Fortuna Investments and an investor in both companies. "It would also avoid redundancy and the time he spends going back and forth between two entities, and there would be a reduction in public company overhead, legal costs and administrative burdens." Analysts have said that [USN:L6N46211S TEXT:"burgeoning capital spending"] for expensive AI and space infrastructure would weigh on SpaceX's free cash flow, a strain a combined company could ease by sharing services and borrowing jointly with Tesla. They also pointed to last week's [USN:L1N46200L TEXT:"Roadster unveiling"], where a Tesla car built with SpaceX rocket thrusters flipped and leapt over vehicles, as a teaser for what a combined company could produce. However, much of the technology on which the lofty valuations of the companies are based, including data centers in orbit, self-driving taxis at scale and humanoid robots, has yet to reach commercial scale. That would take years of heavy spending and engineering, adding execution risk to a deal already facing questions over governance and price. "The big reason why this makes so much sense is that what Tesla is doing SpaceX needs and what SpaceX is doing Tesla needs," Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on X. "And both of them operate under the grand vision which is Elon building a true vertical AI company." PREMIUM - THE NEXT BATTLE Price is likely to be the next fight. Tesla shareholders would be swapping a stake in an independent company, where Musk holds about 20% of the vote, for shares in SpaceX that Musk controls. RBC Capital Markets and JPMorgan analysts expect investors would want a premium of between 20% and 35%, but some do not expect a premium. Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki, whose firm owns both stocks, argues that any premium would dilute SpaceX shareholders as its spending bills rise. Michael Monaghan of Founder ETFs said the overlap between the two shareholder bases means he does not expect a substantial premium. TESLA VOTE IS THE HURDLE Control may also be part of Musk's appeal for a merger. Musk holds about 85% of SpaceX's voting power through super-voting shares. But at Tesla he has roughly 20%. Bill Birmingham, head of research at REX Financial, estimates a merger would give the billionaire about 57% of voting rights. Ryan Zurrer, founder of Dialectic, puts it at 58% at an exchange ratio of 0.7 of one SpaceX share, the illustrative level Barclays has floated. No ratio has been negotiated. Zurrer said a ratio near 0.6 would be needed for Musk to keep control if he sold more equity, and that "the biggest hurdle will be the Tesla shareholders vote vs Elon's own incentives". Musk said Tesla side needs a majority of all shares, not just those voted, so every uncast ballot counts against a deal. Analysts have flagged turnout as a risk, citing uncast broker votes at last year's meeting as a potential factor that could affect chances of a deal going through. Governance and regulatory questions would follow. When Tesla bought SolarCity in 2016, a Delaware court cleared it after years of litigation but said it should have formed an independent committee. "A deal where one man runs both sides will draw tough questions on governance," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at eToro. Tesla is set to report third-quarter results after markets close. Analysts said they were also watching out for disclosures of merger talks in regulatory filings ahead of the automaker's December 3 annual shareholder meeting.

item.title: Colombia to enact 2027 budget by decree after congressional process fails
item.description: Colombia's government said on Wednesday it will enact its 2027 budget of 634.9 trillion pesos ($198.83 billion) by decree after a procedural error in Congress derailed final approval of the bill, testing the new administration's ability to manage public finances and reassure investors.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Colombia's government said on Wednesday it will enact its 2027 budget of 634.9 trillion pesos ($198.83 billion) by decree after a procedural error in Congress derailed final approval of the bill, testing the new administration's ability to manage public finances and reassure investors. The Senate and lower chamber [USN:L6N4660ZT TEXT:"passed different versions"] of the budget bill earlier this week without reconciling the changes, causing lawmakers and legal experts to argue the process was invalid. Vice President Jose Manuel Restrepo said the government's original proposal, together with the amendments previously approved by lawmakers, will now take effect The Senate approved the bill on Monday night and the lower house passed it early Tuesday, but a disputed article was approved with different wording in each chamber and never went through the required conciliation process Colombia is facing widening fiscal pressures - the 2027 spending plan is larger than the 2026 budget of 555.8 trillion pesos and projects a fiscal deficit of 9.4% of gross domestic product Later on Wednesday President Abelardo De La Espriella replaced Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara with Alejandro Ordoñez ($1 = 3,193.1200 Colombian pesos)

item.title: Monitoring the monitors: US states prepare for surge of Justice Dept election watchers
item.description: The Department of Justice plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors in all 50 states on Election Day.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Goudsward, Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
item.content:encoded: When Justice Department staffers arrived in Minnesota this summer to monitor the state's primary election, they found themselves under scrutiny as well. Minnesota officials deployed about 40 state employees, working in pairs, to track the DOJ lawyers as they traveled through two counties during the August vote. The monitoring effort reflected mounting tensions between Minnesota and the Trump administration over [USN:S0N3ZK09X TEXT:"elections"] and [USN:S0N41X003 TEXT:"immigration"]. Democratic Secretary of State Steve Simon said his office is likely to continue coordinating with the state attorney general's office to shadow federal monitors during the November 3 midterms , when control of Congress is at stake. California has launched a similar program. While Simon acknowledged the DOJ monitors were not disruptive, the moves by Minnesota and California nevertheless underscore the unease in Democratic-led and some Republican-led states about the DOJ’s plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors in all 50 states on Election Day, roughly triple the number in the last [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm election"]. The deployment would be the largest observation effort in the department’s history. The Trump administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, [USN:L6N45E0P6 TEXT:"pressing states"] for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including both Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach. “They are the source of interference,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in an interview, referring to the federal government. “They are the ones that are intimidating and creating the suppression.” Justice Department officials accuse critics of fear-mongering about the monitor program, saying it will focus on compliance with civil rights laws as in prior elections. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels said the monitors will be trained not to interfere with election processes and will focus on countering voter intimidation and protecting access. The DOJ has not yet revealed where monitors will be deployed, but department officials said priorities include areas with a history of voter access issues and places with competitive races that could be targets of voter intimidation. The expanded monitor program has led several states to issue new guidelines to local election officials and poll workers about the limited authority DOJ observers will have on Election Day. Some state and local laws allow election officials to prevent DOJ monitors from being present inside polling locations. DOJ staff can observe voting, speak to voters after they leave polling places and report immediate concerns to local law enforcement or election officials. But they cannot conduct investigations on the spot or otherwise stop anyone from voting. In Nevada, the chief election official, [USN:L6N45T0TJ TEXT:"Democrat Cisco Aguilar"], said local law enforcement will be trained to remove any DOJ monitor breaking rules or refusing to leave a polling place if asked. In Maine, where a key race could help decide control of the Senate, the secretary of state has told local election supervisors to contact the state if federal monitors request permission to observe. A LONG-RUNNING PROGRAM The Justice Department for decades has dispatched election monitors to document potential civil rights violations, such as polling locations that lack Spanish-language ballots or are inaccessible to people with disabilities. The Trump administration has [USN:L6N3X91KM TEXT:"reshaped"] the DOJ's Civil Rights Division, which runs the monitoring program, [USN:L1N3TK0O6 TEXT:"prompting an exodus"] of career staff and a new focus on election fraud and voting by non-US citizens. The new emphasis has led some state officials, rights groups and former DOJ lawyers to fear the expanded program could be used as a tool to sow doubt about the security of the election, in which Democrats are widely expected to gain control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. “There’s never been a time when DOJ’s presence would have been viewed as this much of a threat,” said Stacey Young, a former DOJ lawyer who previously worked as an election monitor and now runs Justice Connection, an advocacy group that has opposed the Trump administration. A particular concern among voter rights groups is the department's plan to deploy criminal prosecutors as monitors, in a break with historical practice. The department has relied on civil lawyers and support staff in the past out of concern that the presence of criminal prosecutors at the polls could make voters apprehensive. A major civil rights group, the NAACP, has sued to bar prosecutors and other law enforcement personnel from serving as monitors, arguing the Trump administration's plans amount to voter intimidation. A senior DOJ official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational details, said voters were unlikely to notice a difference between prosecutors and other DOJ staff. "Monitors will not identify themselves as prosecutors," Pels said in a statement, arguing the NAACP lawsuit is based on "unwarranted fear and baseless speculation." She said the monitors would document instances of any alleged voting by noncitizens they uncover, a core Trump administration priority that has not historically been a focus of the program. “If monitors observe any violation of federal election law, including voting by noncitizens, they record and report it to the Department,” Pels said. The senior DOJ official said monitors would not seek to check voters’ citizenship status on Election Day. Reports from monitors, however, could contribute to investigations after the election, the official said. It's unclear what evidence of illegal voting monitors would be able to collect while observing in polling places. The Trump administration has made voting by noncitizens a centerpiece of its campaign alleging voter fraud, [USN:L6N45F10R TEXT:"prosecuting"] alleged offenders in past elections and [USN:SPN45000O TEXT:"seeking to block"] California from counting some 20,000 mail ballots from voters the administration alleges are likely noncitizens. Studies have found that the practice is rare, but President Donald Trump and his allies have held up isolated cases as evidence to falsely claim that US elections are "rigged." FEW INCIDENTS IN PRIMARIES The DOJ has said it monitored hundreds of polling places in 11 states during this year’s primary elections. Few incidents were reported, but in Wyoming, the state’s Republican governor, Mark Gordon, asked the state attorney general to probe what he described as aggressive conduct by DOJ monitors, including requests to examine voting machines. The DOJ official said monitors only asked about the machines to inquire about access for people with disabilities. A spokesperson for Gordon said disagreements remained about the episode. Officials in several states told Reuters they had worked successfully with DOJ monitors in prior elections and did not anticipate disruptions this year. Two Minnesota counties, Hennepin and Ramsey, invoked state law to keep DOJ monitors from within 100 feet (30 meters) of polling places during the primary election in August.

item.title: Trump campaigns in South Carolina to support Senate candidate Graham
item.description: President Donald Trump campaigned in South Carolina on Wednesday to support Republican Senator Darline Graham, who is in a surprisingly competitive Senate race for the seat once held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump campaigned in South Carolina on Wednesday to support Republican Senator Darline Graham, who is in a surprisingly competitive Senate race for the seat once held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham. Less than two weeks before the November 3 election, Darline Graham is running about even in the polls against Democrat Annie Andrews in a state Republicans typically win handily, another sign of the political headwinds confronting Trump's party amid high gasoline prices and the war in Iran . Despite poll numbers showing his popularity at [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"an all-time low"], Trump has campaigned in multiple states in an effort to maintain Republican majorities in Congress. All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake on November 3, with Democrats favored to regain control of the House and be competitive for control of the Senate. Protesters interrupted Trump multiple times during his speech at Clemson University. The crowd chanted "USA" as security guards escorted the protesters out of the arena. Sporadic protests have interrupted proceedings at recent rallies by Trump, who repeatedly cast the demonstrators without evidence as "paid protesters." Trump began his speech at Clemson University with an endorsement of Graham and praised her brother, who died unexpectedly of a heart ailment in July. "I love that brother," Trump said, adding that he used to send Lindsey Graham as an emissary to deal with politicians of either party. "He respected Darline more than any person alive. That included me, and I wasn't happy about it," Trump joked during the rally at a livestock arena. Trump counted Lindsey Graham as one of his closest allies and a foreign policy adviser. He backed Darline Graham to take over her brother's seat after he died and quickly endorsed her bid for a full six-year term, setting off tensions with other Republicans seeking the seat. Trump's rally at Clemson University comes at a complicated moment for Graham. Trump last week waived sanctions on Russia that her brother, a leading Republican advocate for Ukraine, had championed in the months before he died. Trump has been reluctant to punish Russian President Vladimir Putin for the war he started and instead has mounted pressure on Ukraine to make concessions to Moscow to end the conflict. Graham, while otherwise supportive of Trump, has said she disagrees with the president removing the sanctions. "I don't trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia," she told the Associated Press on Saturday. Graham did not mention Russia in a speech before Trump took the stage, instead focusing on the issues that have become a staple of Republican politics, such as opposition to transgender rights, illegal immigration, gun control and abortion. Trump went to South Carolina to help push her over the line. Non-partisan analysts rate South Carolina, a state Trump won in 2024 by nearly 18 percentage points, as either likely Republican or leaning Republican. "The fact that he's coming down to South Carolina days before the election tells you how close the election is," said US Representative Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican. Outside Republican groups have been pouring money into the state, where early voting is underway. They have spent $9.7 million since October 1 to support Graham or attack Andrews, a pediatrician, according to a Reuters analysis of federal campaign filings. By contrast, they have only spent $240,000 on the Senate race in neighboring North Carolina over the same period as Democrat Roy Cooper has established a firm lead over Republican Michael Whatley, despite Trump previously winning the state in all three of his presidential races. Trump's 32-day campaign blitz has largely taken him to Republican-leaning areas that he won comfortably in previous elections, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans as they try to retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives. The [USN:L6N46517O TEXT:"latest Reuters/Ipsos poll"], published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, a record low for the president.

item.title: Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff
item.description: Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Wednesday and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the US, after talks that Washington said were a step toward ending the war in Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia freed [USN:L8N4670PP TEXT:"Stephen Hubbard"], a retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Wednesday and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the US, after talks that Washington said were a step toward ending the war in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue toward planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" in thanking him for the move, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The prisoner release comes as President Donald Trump's recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, have already sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals. Putin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said Putin had freed Hubbard, 74, at Trump's request, and that he had also taken into account the American's poor health. Trump later confirmed he had asked Putin on a call in recent days, and Putin agreed. "The president sends his thanks, our whole nation sends their thanks, because of Stephen Hubbard," Witkoff told Putin in the meeting shown on Russian state TV. "Because of you he's going home to his family." In a video shared with Reuters, Hubbard, wearing a dark fleece and clean-shaven, is seen in an undisclosed location in Russia shaking Witkoff's hand and thanking him. Later, Trump posted a picture of Hubbard appearing inside a plane with others and holding an American flag. Trump told reporters late on Wednesday that Hubbard had landed and that he would be visiting the White House "over the next day or so." Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, told Reuters earlier in a voice message that he spoke briefly by phone with his father before he boarded the airplane in Russia. "Today he seemed light in his step, a sense of happiness in his voice", Coleman said. THREE-WAY MEETING PLANNED ON WAR Witkoff called the talks with Putin "constructive" and said in a post on X that he had also met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo to advance Trump's mission to end the war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he supported the US proposal for three-way talks with Russia and the US at the level of negotiators to be held as soon as possible, preferably by early November. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere, who also met Witkoff, had earlier said the talks will likely happen in mid-November and focus on a potential post-conflict security structure. On Wednesday evening, officials in Kyiv said Russian forces attacked the capital city with ballistic missiles that damaged homes and a petrol station and caused injuries. 'HUMANITARIAN' Witkoff's praise for Putin over Hubbard's release was scorned by some in Washington. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say," Republican US Senator Thom Tillis said in an X post directed at the US envoy. Trump, asked about Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment earlier on Wednesday, told reporters at the White House: “Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man, who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out. But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other." The US "gave nothing in exchange" for the prisoner release, Trump said, adding "we're getting closer" to settling the war. "He is the happiest man around," Trump said of Hubbard. "This was very surprising to him, but I did it, it really took place on a phone call at the end of last week with President Putin, so we appreciate it very much. And his family is extremely happy." FAMILY, LAWYER DISPUTED CONVICTION Hubbard, a native of Michigan, had been serving a prison sentence of six years and 10 months in Russia following a conviction for mercenary activity in a closed-door trial. He was arrested in April 2022 in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum, where Russian prosecutors alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media reported he pleaded guilty to the charges. But Hubbard's US-based lawyer, Martin De Luca, previously told Reuters that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. In a 2024 interview with Reuters, Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, also disputed the idea that her brother took up arms for any government, calling him "so non-military" and pointing out his advanced age. De Luca on Wednesday thanked Trump, Witkoff and other US officials for securing the release, calling it "a dividend earned along the hard road to peace". As of Wednesday, Hubbard was the only US prisoner held by Russia who was designated by Washington as "wrongfully detained". The Trump administration secured the release last year of another American jailed in Russia, schoolteacher [USN:S0N3P202G TEXT:"Marc Fogel"], who had been serving a 14-year prison term for drug smuggling.

item.title: Putin agrees to resume 3-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
item.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two. The negotiations in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia - the release of [USN:L8N4670PP TEXT:"Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher"] held in Russia whom US President Trump had asked the Kremlin chief to release. Wednesday's encounter unfolded amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications. The latest talks also came more than two years since Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours. The Kremlin said the new 3-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. They could begin sometime on or after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran . The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. Witkoff told Putin the talks had been characterised by "some degree of momentum" and a US official said Ukraine had brought [USN:L1N466099 TEXT:"new ideas and proposals"]. "These nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting - which lasted nearly three hours. POSSIBLE MEETING BETWEEN TRUMP, PUTIN AND XI Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, though Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing." Putin also used Wednesday's talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear programme. Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said. Russia could also supply vast quantities of fertiliser to the United States to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff. [USN:L1N4650BJ TEXT:"A potential meeting in China next month"] with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history. 'NEW IDEAS' Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no NATO membership for Kyiv, and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire. Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy, was also present at the talks with Witkoff and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, including some that were close to being realised. Witkoff said he had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone. Zelenskiy said he [USN:L1N4670EW TEXT:"hoped to discuss key issues"] on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump. The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskiy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile. FRAYING US-UKRAINE TIES US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections. Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelenskiy said that Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues. Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

item.title: Government websites go dark after AI-discovered flaw sparks security scramble
item.description: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language that sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Leo Marchandon, Kanjyik Ghosh, Rajveer Pardesi
item.content:encoded: Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems. Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying all users were "encouraged to update immediately." With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took sites offline as a precaution. Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates. AI was powering a "race to exploit," said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet." PHP — a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page" — underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences. "All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable," said Tiffany Farriss, the interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. "This issue impacts the majority of the internet." Cybersecurity agencies around the world have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. According to data from Censys, the internet intelligence firm, about 1.5 million out of 2.6 million hosts report running a version of PHP for which there is no fix. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched, while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it also briefly went offline to deal with the issue. Even some world leaders weighed in. The Dutch prime minister said he was closely monitoring the situation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a post on X said website owners should "check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix." BUG FOUND WITH AI The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, two cybersecurity companies said in independent reports. Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on August 1 and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned (GOOGL.O) cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz's post said. "Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale," it said. "With AI, this is no longer a barrier." Calif and Wiz said they coordinated with one another and the PHP team and OpenAI on the discovery. In a statement, the White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday. In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon (AMZN.O) security chief CJ Moses said the tech giant's security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy "honeypot" systems on October 17, four days before public disclosure. The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo. More attempts followed on Wednesday by multiple actors before the embargo lifted. Amazon said it was still unclear whether any of the attempts would have worked against real websites, adding the flaws were "now being broadly exploited in the wild." CRITICAL SOFTWARE PHP is a [USN:L6N467127 TEXT:"programming language"] used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers. Its ubiquity — PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs — has made experts anxious. AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have [USN:L6N46118G TEXT:"proliferated in recent weeks"], could wreak havoc on unpatched servers, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London. "The scale is huge, and with AI, exploitation may happen instantly," Olejnik said. WordPress.com operator Automattic said users of its hosted solutions and Tumblr were safe from the bug . Risks were higher for small PHP-powered websites run by individuals or organizations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly manage the underlying servers. MASS OUTAGES In the Netherlands, several organizations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national soccer association KNVB, the websites for the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites. Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform. Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure." France's Interior Ministry said it had placed all of its websites into preventive maintenance.

item.title: Beauty giants target 'Ozempic face' as boom in obesity drugs opens new market
item.description: Swiss skincare firm Galderma , Brazilian cosmetics group Natura and beauty giant L'Oreal are testing treatments for consumers worried about facial sagging and volume loss, looking to capitalise on a growing market tied to the boom in obesity drugs.
item.dc:creator: Richa Naidu, Dominique Patton, Alexander Marrow
item.content:encoded: Swiss skincare firm Galderma (GALD.S) , Brazilian cosmetics group Natura (NATU3m.BA) and beauty giant L'Oreal (OREP.PA) are testing treatments for consumers worried about facial sagging and volume loss, looking to capitalise on a growing market tied to the boom in obesity drugs. This is the third story in a five-part Reuters series on how weight-loss drugs are changing the way people shop and eat, and how companies are responding to the trend. The companies are targeting concerns known as "Ozempic face," a term that emerged as the diabetes drug became widely associated with weight loss. Experts say the loss of facial volume is linked to rapid weight loss rather than GLP-1 drugs themselves. GLP-1 drugs, such as Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's (LLY.N) Zepbound, help people to lose weight by mimicking a hormone that keeps the stomach feeling full. Along with gastrointestinal side effects, the resulting rapid weight loss can also lead to loose skin on the face and body. Pfizer estimates the obesity drug market could reach $150 billion in annual sales by 2030, helping create a potentially lucrative opportunity for skincare and medical aesthetics companies as more patients seek treatments for skin laxity and facial volume loss after rapid weight loss. Revenue from these clinical treatments is projected to grow from about $700 million to $2 billion over the next five years, according to 2025 estimates by Boston Consulting Group. Michael Somenek, a Washington, DC-based facial plastic surgeon and clinical associate professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine, said he had seen a surge of requests for treatment by GLP-1 patients in the past year. "When you're looking at a large amount of weight loss over four to six months, that can really have impact on the volume within your face," he said. COMPANIES CHASE THE OPPORTUNITY Galderma, 20%-owned by L'Oreal, ran a study last year evaluating how some of its existing treatments perform on skin changes associated with GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. "Sagginess is a concern, loss of firmness is a concern, some hollowness can be of concern and dullness can be a concern," said Anne-Cecile Chevrier, global head of injectable aesthetics at Galderma. The Swiss company makes Sculptra, a treatment that stimulates natural collagen, and Restylane, a dermal filler made with hyaluronic acid. Chevrier said that although the treatments were not approved specifically for GLP-1 users, Galderma is working with tens of thousands of plastic surgeons and other aestheticians globally who market them to patients on weight-loss drugs. In the United States, 53% of aesthetics clinics anticipate an influx of new patients due to prescription weight-loss medications, according to a 2024 report by research firm Medical Insight, and 43% believe the increased use of these medications will drive demand for treatments addressing weight-loss-medication-induced facial changes. L'Oreal is also exploring this market. "We are now testing products on GLP-1 users in separate studies, as this group of consumers is becoming increasingly important and represents a significant number of people worldwide," said Delphine Viguier-Hovasse, L'Oreal's chief innovation and prospective officer. Manuel Krauss, Natura's chief innovation and R&D officer, said the company is testing existing products directly with GLP-1 users and developing a new generation of treatments. "GLP-1 is creating new beauty needs at unprecedented speed, but it is also showing us that the future of beauty cannot be defined by creams alone," Krauss said, noting that future innovation may combine different formats such as supplements and ingestibles. A MORE COMPLICATED PICTURE Other factors can be at play in patients experiencing skin or facial volume issues. According to analysts at the US health policy organisation KFF, GLP-1 drugs are used most widely by adults aged 50 to 64, an age group already experiencing declines in collagen and, particularly among menopausal women, estrogen production. "We don't have the research and it is probably going to be a challenging study to do because most of the female patients (on GLP-1 drugs) are perimenopausal or postmenopausal," said Heidi Young, a Northern California-based physician associate and co-owner of R+H Aesthetic Medicine. She added that some people taking GLP-1 drugs do not eat nutritious food often, which could also affect their skin: "I think it's definitely multifactorial and I don't think there is a direct answer." DO THE PRODUCTS WORK? Beibei Du-Harpur, a consultant dermatologist and clinical lecturer at King’s College London, said the term "Ozempic face" is misleading. “The drug doesn’t melt your collagen — simply losing weight in a more sustainable, less rapid way would reduce some of the more severe changes people see." Experts said some skincare products may improve the appearance and quality of skin affected but cannot fully address the underlying loss of facial volume. "To a certain extent some of these creams can be helpful," said Dr Graeme Glass, plastic and craniofacial surgeon and aesthetic director at British beauty brand LYMA. Creams can work on the epidermis and contain molecules small enough to reach the dermis. "What they can't really do is they can't alter the ligamental structure of your face," he said. "They can't reposition the deep fat pads of the face ... there is a limit to what these things can do." Du-Harpur said beauty companies were "all desperately trying to develop a GLP-1-targeting product." She said treatments such as fillers that use injections worked better than creams as they could reach the dermis, the middle and thickest layer of human skin. “What’s actually losing volume is the layer below that – the fat layer – and there has never been any evidence that topical skincare products can reach that fat layer." item.title: Woodside Energy trims output forecast, to pull back from US ammonia project
item.description: Australia's Woodside Energy on Wednesday trimmed the top end of its annual production forecast and said it would scale back its investment in a lower-carbon ammonia project in the US due to slower demand.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia's Woodside Energy (WDS.AX) on Wednesday trimmed the top end of its annual production forecast and said it would scale back its investment in a lower-carbon ammonia project in the US due to slower demand. The country's top independent oil and gas producer now expects annual production of 174 to 181 million barrels of oil equivalent (boe), down from its earlier forecast of 174 to 185 million boe. The scaled-back ammonia investment is the latest step back from clean energy at Woodside, which under CEO Liz Westcott has [USN:L4N44L1IT TEXT:"abandoned one of its longer-term emissions targets"] and canned $5 billion in planned lower carbon spending. The Beaumont New Ammonia plant in Texas brought in lower-than-expected volumes for the quarter, with production constrained to 69% of capacity due to third-party feedstock availability and a 30-day shutdown following a safety incident. Woodside said it would reduce its investment in the plant after completing a strategic review that found customer demand was slower than expected. "The policy frameworks that were going to enable the lower carbon ammonia to be part of that market are also shifting," Westcott added. Woodside acquired the plant for $2.35 billion in 2024 as part of a green energy push under former CEO Meg O'Neill. Westcott said Woodside was focused on developing other parts of its portfolio such as the long-delayed [USN:L4N41O082 TEXT:"Browse liquefied natural gas project"] off Western Australia, which could supply a range of customers including data centre operators and critical minerals producers. "There's been a lot of interest in Browse in the last 12 months," Westcott said, while adding there was also interest from potential equity partners. Environmental approvals and negotiations over a processing agreement have delayed Browse's progress. Westcott said she was comfortable with how Browse's emissions were being addressed in its approval assessments in light of concerns a [USN:L1N45T02K TEXT:"recent decision from Australia's top court"], blocking a coal mine on climate grounds, could impact approvals of fossil fuel projects across the country. Woodside reported revenue of $4.28 billion for the three months ended September 30, up from $3.36 billion reported a year ago , beating a Visible Alpha consensus of $4.11 billion. Its average realised price for its products rose 40% from a year earlier to $84 per barrel of oil equivalent. Quarterly production volumes fell 9% from a year earlier to 46.2 mmboe, but rose 12% from the previous quarter following higher production from Pluto LNG. The company had earlier [USN:L4N43U2QX TEXT:"narrowed its annual production forecast in July"], citing strong operational performance. It also maintained its 2026 capital expenditure outlook at $4 billion to $4.5 billion.

item.description: Wall Street grimpe, aidée par l'appétit pour l'IA
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Wall Street grimpe, aidée par l'appétit pour l'IA 21 octobre (Reuters) - La Bourse de New York a fini en hausse mercredi, après la publication des résultats trimestriels de SpaceX et de Super Micro Computer, qui ont redynamisé l'appétit des investisseurs pour les titres liés à l'intelligence artificielle (IA), au lendemain de pertes enregistrées par le secteur technologique. Etats-Unis: Meta condamné à verser $25 mds pour manquements à la protection de données lors de la présidentielle 2016 21 octobre (Reuters) - Un tribunal du Nouveau-Mexique a ordonné mercredi à Meta de verser 25 milliards de dollars de pénalités pour manquements à la protection de la vie privée, après qu'un jury a déclaré coupable en septembre le géant technologique d'avoir induit en erreur les consommateurs à propos de leurs données. Meta: Émission de nouvelles actions, prévisions supérieures aux attentes au T4 21 octobre (Reuters) - Meta a dit mercredi prévoir pour le trimestre actuel un chiffre d'affaires supérieur aux attentes et a annoncé son intention d'émettre de nouvelles actions sans droit de vote, une mesure qui devrait contribuer à financer son expansion coûteuse dans le domaine de l'intelligence artificielle (IA). Edenred-Le dépassement des attentes au T3 peine à convaincre, le titre baisse 21 octobre (Reuters) - Edenred a publié mercredi un revenu total supérieur aux attentes au titre du troisième trimestre, le spécialiste français des titres-restaurant citant la croissance continue de son segment mobilité. Covivio: Hausse de 2,7% des revenus sur les neufs premiers mois 21 octobre (Reuters) - Covivio a fait état mercredi d'une croissance de 2,7% de ses revenus à périmètre constant sur les neufs premiers mois de son exercice, soutenus entre autres par les hausses de loyers et les gains de taux d'occupation ainsi que les revenus variables des hôtels. FDJ United abaisse ses objectifs de CA et de produit brut des jeux 21 octobre (Reuters) - FDJ United a annoncé mercredi un abaissement de ses objectifs annuels, tablant désormais sur une baisse comprise entre 1% et 3% ("low-single digit") du produit brut des jeux (PBJ) et sur un déclin d'environ 5% ("mid-single digit") de son chiffre d'affaires pour l'exercice 2026. Le rendement de l'OAT à 10 ans atteint 5% pour la première fois depuis juillet 2002 21 octobre (Reuters) - Le rendement de l'obligation souveraine française à 10 ans a atteint mercredi le seuil psychologique de 5% pour la première fois depuis juillet 2002, ce qui constitue un nouveau signe de l'inquiétude des investisseurs quant à la capacité de la deuxième économie de la zone euro à réduire son déficit. Moncler: CA stable au T3, freiné par la baisse des dépenses touristiques en Europe MILAN, 21 octobre (Reuters) - Moncler a fait état mercredi d'un chiffre d'affaires globalement stable au troisième trimestre à taux directeur constants, le groupe italien de vêtements de luxe subissant les effets d'un recul en Europe lié à la baisse des dépenses touristiques. Eurofins Scientific ajuste ses objectifs 2026, CA à neuf mois +3,7% 21 octobre (Reuters) - Eurofins Scientific a ajusté mercredi ses objectifs financiers pour l'exercice en cours, citant notamment des conditions de marché restant plus atones que d'ordinaire. OPmobility: CA consolidé à +2,8% au T3, tiré par l'ensemble des segments 21 octobre (Reuters) - OPmobility a fait état mercredi d'un chiffre d'affaires consolidé en hausse de 2,8% à périmètre et changes constants au troisième trimestre de son exercice, à 2,44 milliards d'euros, l'équipementier automobile français citant la croissance de l'ensemble de ses segments.

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: Etats-Unis: Des chaînes de télévision accusées de relayer de "faux sondages" avant les 'midterms'
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Etats-Unis: Des chaînes de télévision accusées de relayer de "faux sondages" avant les 'midterms' WASHINGTON, 21 octobre (Reuters) - Le patron de la Commission fédérale des communications (FCC), chargée notamment d'attribuer et superviser les licences accordées aux chaînes de télévision aux Etats-Unis, a déclaré mercredi que des chaînes diffusaient "des sondages totalement faux", constituant une possible violation de leurs obligations. L'Irak ferme le point de passage de Sheeb avec l'Iran BASRA, 21 octobre (Reuters) - - L'Irak a fermé le point de passage de Sheeb avec l'Iran pour des raisons de sécurité et dans le but d'installer des équipements de détection empêchant le passage de marchandises interdites, a annoncé vendredi un responsable des services frontaliers irakiens. La députée australienne attaquée par une voiture amputée des deux jambes SYDNEY, 21 octobre (Reuters) - La députée australienne Helen Haines, qui a été délibérément percutée par une voiture devant son bureau lundi, a dû être amputée des deux jambes, a déclaré mercredi son mari. Poutine annonce la libération d'un professeur retraité américain lors de sa rencontre avec Witkoff SAINT-PÉTERSBOURG, Russie, 21 octobre (Reuters) - Stephen Hubbard, professeur américain retraité de 74 ans emprisonné en Russie depuis 2022, a été libéré de prison et est en route vers l'aéroport Poulkovo de Saint-Pétersbourg, a annoncé mercredi le président russe Vladimir Poutine. La première cargaison de diesel russe expédiée aux États-Unis jeudi, dit Moscou MOSCOU, 21 octobre (Reuters) - - La Russie va expédier jeudi son premier pétrolier transportant du diesel à destination des Etats-Unis, a annoncé mercredi le vice-premier ministre russe Alexander Novak, cité par le journal Vedomosti. Italie: Les commerçants préviennent de pénuries alimentaires dues au mouvement des routiers ROME, 21 octobre (Reuters) - Des pénuries alimentaires pourraient voir le jour en Italie en raison du mouvement de protestation des routiers italiens contre les prix du carburant et le coût de la vie, les livraisons étant perturbées, ont dit mercredi les commerçants du pays. Italie: Le gouvernement instaure des lois anti-émeute plus strictes ROME, 20 octobre (Reuters) - Le gouvernement italien a adopté mardi une série de mesures sécuritaires face aux manifestations violentes dans le pays, dont la création d'une nouvelle infraction en la matière, un durcissement des sanctions contre les émeutiers et l'instauration d'une responsabilité financière de parents dont les enfants se livreraient à des pillages et du vandalisme. Ukraine-Zelensky doit rencontrer Witkoff pour relancer la relation avec Washington Volodimir Zelensky doit rencontrer mardi en Norvège l'envoyé spécial américain Steve Witkoff dans l'espoir de relancer les relations bilatérales avec les Etats-Unis, qui se sont détériorées encore davantage depuis que Donald Trump a appelé à la démission du homologue ukrainien. Roumanie-Un Premier ministre enfin en poste, après des mois de blocage Le Parlement roumain a confirmé l'indépendant Luca Niculescu au poste de Premier ministre mardi, mettant fin à une crise politique de six mois qui a pesé sur la note de crédit du pays et ébranlé la confiance des investisseurs. Le vol des téléphones portables, enjeu électoral majeur La créatrice de contenu brésilienne Tabata Lenk venait tout juste d'être licenciée quand, coincée dans les bouchons de Sao Paulo, deux hommes à moto brisent la fenêtre passager de sa voiture pour lui arracher son smartphone flambant neuf accroché sur le tableau de bord de sa voiture.
